blocks.text: Machine learning mechanisms describe how systems learn from data. Different mechanisms are used for different problems. Some methods use labeled data, while others do not (as shown in Figure 6.4).

blocks.alt: Two tables side by side. Left, LABELED DATA, 'Data with labels (outputs) that tell us what the data is.': columns Image and Label, rows apple - Apple, banana - Banana, orange - Orange, grapes - Grapes; below: 'Used in supervised learning (e.g., classification, regression)'. Right, UNLABELED DATA, 'Data without labels. We don't know what the data is.': a 4 by 3 grid of the same fruit pictures in mixed order with no labels; below: 'Used in unsupervised learning (e.g., clustering, association)'.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: Labeled vs Unlabeled Data (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.4)
blocks.long_description: Every picture on the left has its name beside it; the pictures on the right have no names.

blocks.text: Certain methods are learned through feedback and experience. Each mechanism follows a different learning process. Choosing the correct mechanism is important. The quality of learning depends on the method used. These mechanisms support intelligent decision-making. Machine learning systems rely on proper mechanisms to work effectively. Some kinds of machine learning are discussed below:

Supervised machine learning uses labeled data for training. Each data item has an input and a correct output. The system learns by comparing its output with the correct answer. Supervised learning needs large labelled datasets, such as emails labelled as spam or not spam, images labelled as cat or dog, or medical scans labelled as normal or abnormal. Its accuracy usually improves when the model is trained on more high-quality examples. It is widely used in real applications, such as face recognition, disease detection, speech recognition, fraud detection, and recommendation systems. This method is used for prediction tasks. Examples include email spam detection and exam result prediction.

Unsupervised machine learning works with unlabeled data. The system finds patterns without guidance. It groups similar data together and makes clusters. This method is useful for discovering hidden structures. No correct output is provided. Learning depends on data similarity. Unsupervised learning helps understand data behavior. It is useful for data exploration. Examples include customer grouping and data clustering.

Reinforcement machine learning learns through experience and mimics the human learning. The system interacts with an environment. It receives rewards or penalties for actions. Positive rewards encourage correct behavior. The system improves decision making over time. This method is used in robotics and games. Learning continues through trial and error. The goal is to maximize rewards. Examples of reinforcement learning include a robot learning to navigate a maze through rewards and penalties, AlphaGo improving its strategy by playing Go, an autonomous car optimizing its driving decisions, and a movie recommendation system adjusting its suggestions based on user feedback.
